rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report a four-year field deployment (2017-2020) of an in-situ infrared-radiometer CWSI IoT DSS at two commercial vineyards in Idaho, with own LWP, soil moisture and irrigation measurements.
rows.notes: The study shows that canopy-temperature (infrared radiometer) CWSI identified vine water stress (significant correlations with LWP and fASW, Fig. 7) and that managers used it daily to schedule irrigation (Section 4.4). It reports no yield or grape quality data at all, so it cannot support 'maintain yield and grape quality'. Also no spatial 'stress zones' were mapped: two to four point radiometers in a single vine row, not remote imagery. Supports only the upstream step (stress detection informing irrigation).

rows.evidence: Q1: Own field deployment and measurements over four seasons at two vineyards (Sections 2.1-2.2, Fig. 7, Table 2).
rows.notes: The study integrates CWSI with in-situ weather data, but uses fixed point infrared radiometers, not thermal imagery, and does not identify stress zones (no spatial mapping; sensors in one vine row). It reports no grape quality or yield results. Own results are limited to CWSI-LWP-fASW correlations and manager use of the DSS for scheduling. Technology (thermal imagery/zone mapping) differs and the effect (preserving quality and yield) is not measured; only the upstream step (stress detection guiding irrigation) is shown.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own four-year field study with sensor, LWP and irrigation data (Sections 2-3).
rows.notes: Study is in southwestern Idaho, not Chile, and uses wired sensors with a cellular modem and a neural-network/energy-balance CWSI on a data logger rather than a WSN. No water savings are quantified: there is no comparison with pre-DSS or non-DSS irrigation; Table 2 only reports seasonal irrigation amounts (66-143 mm) and their year-to-year consistency. No grape quality (sugar, acidity) data reported. The '25% savings' figure does not come from this study. Shows only that the DSS monitors vine water status and was used for scheduling, a precondition for savings.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own four-year field deployment with measured CWSI, LWP, fASW and irrigation (Sections 2-3).
rows.notes: No grape quality or yield parameters (sugar content, acidity, cluster weight) were measured or reported in this study; the only reference to cluster weight is a cited earlier study [19] in the Introduction, which does not count. Site is Idaho, not Chile. The study shows only that the IoT DSS tracked vine water status and was used daily for irrigation decisions.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own field deployment at two commercial vineyards over 2017-2020 with sensor, LWP and irrigation measurements (Sections 2.1-2.2). Q2: Table 2, Section 4.4 and Abstract: seasonal average daily CWSI (0.23-0.31 at V-A, 0.36-0.44 at V-B) and cumulative irrigation were consistent across the four years despite yearly differences in evaporative demand and precipitation (Table 1), which the authors take as evidence that managers used the DSS to maintain a consistent deficit irrigation program under varying climatic conditions. Q4: Fig. 7 and Section 3.2: the intermediate variable, vine water status, was measured directly by midday LWP and by fASW and shown to be significantly correlated (p<0.001) with the DSS CWSI; Fig. 8 shows CWSI, fASW and LWP responding together to irrigation and rainfall events. Q6: Sections 2.1 and 4.4: deployed on two commercial estate vineyards (<7 ha farms) where the vineyard managers, not researchers, used the DSS daily to schedule irrigation for the operation. Q7: Section 4.5: authors state from their own data that solar radiation must exceed about 200 W m-2 and the canopy must be dry for valid CWSI (values below zero otherwise), that the models are valid only within the weather range of the training database (e.g. wind speeds below 5 m s-1), and that the approach works provided reference temperatures can be reliably estimated. Q8: Section 4.5: limited to two small vineyards in one semiarid region; models may not perform elsewhere; CWSI errors under rain/low radiation; equipment too expensive for commercial use and monitors a single location; LWP sometimes not on the same vines and taken under variable clouds (Section 4.3).
rows.notes: Q2 given with caution: the study's own result is interannual consistency of CWSI and irrigation under year-to-year climatic variability (not long-term climate change), and 'resilience and productivity' were not measured (no yield data). Q3: the consistency result rests on one measurement method (sensor-derived CWSI and metered irrigation); manager self-reports confirm use, not the effect. Q6 is marginal: the deployment is at farm scale with manager-level scheduling, but sensors and irrigation metering were at a single vine-row location. Q9: Table 2 gives seasonal means without SD or CI; Table 1 SDs refer to 20-yr climate, not the result. The study is in Idaho, not Chile, and is not a WSN per se.

notes: Full text available and apparently complete. The study is a four-year deployment of an in-situ infrared radiometer CWSI IoT decision support system at two small commercial vineyards in Idaho; it reports no yield, grape quality or water-savings data, no thermal imagery, and no Chilean site, so it mismatches most of the claims it is cited for (the '[70]' citations appear to attribute results of another study to it).
